unit.title: Produce management reports to enable effective decision making

summary: This unit teaches you to produce management reports that help managers make decisions: find out what the decision is and who needs what, choose the right type of report, use accurate and consistent data, pick relevant costs, analyse make-or-buy, special-order, limiting-factor, closure, pricing and investment decisions, interpret results, state assumptions and test them, present findings clearly, and handle confidentiality and ethics.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. A **management report** is information prepared inside an organisation to help its managers plan, control and decide. It is different from the annual financial statements, which follow a fixed format and are written mainly for owners, lenders and the tax authority.

Accountants, finance officers and managers in Jamaican hotels, manufacturers, distributors, schools, agencies and municipal corporations are asked questions such as: 'Should we make or buy this part?', 'Should we accept this one-off order?', 'Should we close this branch?', 'Which products should get the scarce machine time?' Your report must give a clear, correct and honest answer, in a form busy managers can use.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Find out what managers need
Agree the decision, the readers, the deadline and the criteria before you start.
Choose the right type of report
Routine, exception, ad hoc decision, dashboard; the right detail for each reader.
Use accurate, consistent data
Trace figures to the records, cover the same period, restate or note changes.
Select relevant costs
Separate relevant from sunk, committed and apportioned costs; include opportunity costs.
Analyse common decisions
Make or buy, special orders, limiting factors, closing a branch, pricing, investment, working capital.
Interpret results
Compare with budget, last year and similar firms; explain margins, variances and unit costs.
State assumptions and test them
Show the assumptions and use sensitivity analysis; add non-financial factors.
Present and behave professionally
Write a clear report with an executive summary and recommendation; keep it confidential and fair.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions and calculations (contribution, relevant cost, unit cost, variances, ratios).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as relevant cost, limiting factor, sensitivity analysis, executive summary) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** done in a group: a product-line profitability report with a recommendation, and a decision report presented to a management panel, including sensitivity tests.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by a different route, and state the units (J$ per unit, J$ per hour, J$ per month). A correct figure with a wrong unit can still mislead a manager.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Information needs and types of report

blocks.p: The first step is to ask the manager **which decision the report must support**. Do not copy last year's layout, include every figure the system can produce, or begin by choosing colours and charts. Agree: the decision, the options, the deadline, the criteria that matter (return, cash needs, risk, strategy), and the level of detail.

head: Management reports
Financial statements
rows: Shaped to help managers plan, control and decide
Follow a fixed format (set by company law and accounting standards)
Many times a year, even daily
Normally once a year
For managers inside the business
For owners, lenders, the tax authority
May include forecasts and non-financial data
Based mostly on past, recorded transactions

head: Type
Purpose
Example
rows: Routine report
Regular, same layout, monitoring
Monthly sales and cost report
Exception report
Shows only items outside agreed limits, such as costs more than 5% over budget
Overtime 40% over budget at one branch
Ad hoc (decision) report
A one-off report on a particular question
Should we open a new branch in Mandeville?
Dashboard
One page of key measures, often with red/amber/green signals
Daily sales, cash balance, orders, absence
Analytical report
Explains why results changed
Why gross margin fell from 38% to 31%
Aged receivables report
Shows amounts owed by customers by age
Which customers to chase this week

blocks.p: Match the report to the reader. Store managers need **daily detail** on their store; the board needs a **monthly summary**. Giving the same 40-page report to everyone helps nobody.

blocks.note: An exception report saves time but the writer should still add the likely cause and its effect. A figure alone ('overtime 40% over budget') does not tell a manager what to do.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A decision is only as good as its figures. Before you send a report, check the data.

ul: **Trace key figures to the accounting records** (the general ledger, trial balance, bank statements, stock records). Do not ask the reader whether it looks right, or round everything to the nearest million.

**If a total in the report differs from the ledger** (for example, sales J$350,000 different), find and fix the cause before sending. Do not send it and explain next month, change the ledger to match the report, or delete the total.
**Cover the same period** when you combine data from different systems, such as sales from the tills and costs from the accounting system. Otherwise margins are wrong.

**Be consistent**: if a branch changed how it codes costs half-way through the year, restate the figures on one basis or note the change clearly. Do not compare silently, leave the branch out or ask it to change back.
**Reconcile** control totals (for example, to the trial balance) and record any difference you cannot explain.
**Say where each figure came from** and its date.

blocks.p: Include the information that bears on the decision and leave out the rest. For a courier firm deciding whether to add a night shift, the relevant information is the extra contribution from more deliveries set against the shift's extra costs. The total cost of the head office building over ten years, or the number of deliveries by each driver in 2015, does not bear on it.

A decision looks to the future. A **relevant cost** is a **future cash cost that changes as a result of the decision**. Costs that are the same whatever you decide are not relevant, and including them can make a good option look bad or a poor one look good.

head: Cost
Meaning
In a decision report
rows: Sunk cost
Already spent; cannot be recovered
Ignore (a J$2,000,000 feasibility study already paid for)
Committed cost
Must be paid anyway under an earlier agreement, such as a lease
Ignore (it does not change with the decision)
Avoidable cost
Would be saved if an activity, branch or product were stopped
Relevant
Opportunity cost
The benefit given up by choosing one option instead of another
Relevant (rent given up on a warehouse used for a new project)
Incremental cost
Extra cost caused by the decision
Relevant
Apportioned (shared) overhead
A share of common costs charged to a unit
Relevant only if it would really change
Depreciation
An accounting charge, not a cash cost
Usually not relevant; the cash cost of the asset is what matters

ul: **Owned warehouse:** if the firm could rent it out for J$300,000 a month, the relevant cost of using it for a new project is **J$300,000 a month** (the rent given up), not nil and not its purchase price or depreciation.

**Staff time:** engineers are fully booked on client work that earns a contribution of J$6,000 an hour after their pay, and their pay (J$2,500 an hour) will be paid either way. For 50 hours the relevant cost is 50 x J$6,000 = J$300,000, the contribution given up. If the staff were idle, the relevant cost would be nil.
**Materials already in stock** for which there is no other use: the relevant cost may be nil; if they could be sold or used elsewhere, the relevant cost is their resale or replacement value.

blocks.p: **Contribution** = selling price - variable cost. It is the amount each unit adds towards fixed costs and profit. The **contribution-to-sales (C/S) ratio** = contribution / sales x 100. A product selling at J$800 with variable cost of J$560 has contribution of J$240 and a ratio of 240 / 800 = 30%. A case of juice that sells for J$2,500 with variable cost J$1,750 gives J$750 contribution (30%).
If fixed costs will not change, a decision is judged by the **change in total contribution**. This is simple and avoids being misled by apportioned fixed costs.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Fixed costs
Do not change in total, in the short term, with output
Variable costs
Change in total in direct proportion to output
Unit cost
Total cost / number of units; for example J$1,350,000 / 9,000 room-nights = J$150 per room-night

blocks.note: Use unit costs with care. A unit cost that includes fixed costs changes with the volume, so it is a poor guide to what an extra unit will cost.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Common decisions and how to report them

blocks.p: Compare the **relevant** cost of making with the price of buying. If fixed costs will continue whichever option is chosen, ignore them.

ul: A part costs J$420 a unit in variable cost to make. A supplier offers it at J$470. For 10,000 units, buying costs J$500,000 more: **profit falls by J$500,000**.
If making uses equipment that could be rented out for J$150,000 a year, add that opportunity cost to making.

blocks.p: Also state **non-financial factors**: the supplier's reliability, quality control, delivery times, loss of skills, risk of the supplier raising prices, and what happens to the staff.

If there is **spare capacity** and fixed costs will not change, accept a special order if its price is above the variable cost. A hotel kitchen offered 400 conference meals at J$1,500 each, with variable cost of J$1,150 per meal, gains 400 x J$350 = J$140,000.

But the report must mention risks: regular customers may ask for the same lower price; capacity may be needed for normal work; and if capacity is **not** spare, the contribution given up on regular orders is a cost.
When one resource is scarce (machine hours, skilled labour, space), rank the products by **contribution per unit of the scarce resource**, not by contribution per unit of product.

head: Product
Contribution per unit (J$)
Hours per unit
Contribution per hour (J$)
Rank
rows: A
B

blocks.p: Product A earns J$300 an hour against J$225 for B, so A has priority, even though B earns more per unit. Method: (1) calculate contribution per hour for each product; (2) rank them; (3) make the top-ranked product up to its demand; (4) use the remaining hours on the next product; (5) calculate the total contribution.

blocks.h: Closing a branch, line or department

blocks.p: Compare what would be lost with what would be saved. A branch has contribution of J$1,200,000 and its own fixed costs of J$900,000 (which would stop if it closed). It is also charged J$500,000 of head office costs that will continue. The branch report shows a loss of J$200,000 (1,200,000 - 900,000 - 500,000). But if it closes, the company loses its J$1,200,000 contribution and saves only the J$900,000 it avoids, so **profit falls by J$300,000**. Shared costs that continue must not be used to justify closure.
Also report non-financial effects: customers, staff, the firm's name, the effect on other branches, and alternatives such as raising prices, cutting costs or changing opening hours.

Compare total contribution before and after. A restaurant cuts a meal price from J$2,000 to J$1,800 and expects monthly sales to rise from 1,000 to 1,200 meals. Variable cost is J$1,200. Before: (2,000 - 1,200) x 1,000 = J$800,000. After: (1,800 - 1,200) x 1,200 = J$720,000. Contribution **falls** by J$80,000, so the cut is not worthwhile on these figures.

head: Measure
How calculated
Example
rows: Return on capital (ROI) = profit / capital x 100
Yearly profit divided by capital used
Payback
Years to recover the cost from the cash flow
Cost J$6,000,000, cash flow J$1,500,000 a year: 4 years
Net present value (NPV)
Future cash flows discounted to today's value, less cost
Used in larger investment decisions; money received later is worth less

blocks.p: A bigger profit does not mean a better return on the capital. Also report risk, the funding and the effect on cash.

ul: **Inventory days** = inventory / cost of sales x 365. Inventory J$1,500,000 and cost of sales J$9,125,000: 1,500,000 / 9,125,000 x 365 = 60 days.
**Receivable days** = receivables / credit sales x 365.
**Payable days** = payables / purchases (or cost of sales) x 365.

**Gross margin** = (sales - cost of sales) / sales x 100. If gross margin falls from 38% to 31% while sales rise, investigate first whether the **cost of goods rose or prices were cut** (or the sales mix changed). Rent or interest would not affect gross margin.
**Sales value up 15% but units up only 2%:** prices rose or customers bought dearer items.
**Unit cost** = cost / units: laundry J$1,350,000 for 9,000 room-nights is J$150 per room-night.

blocks.p: **Variance** = actual - budget. Costs above budget are **adverse**; below budget are **favourable**. Electricity budget J$850,000, actual J$935,000: J$85,000 **adverse**, which is 85,000 / 850,000 = 10% over budget.

A good report explains each significant variance: **what happened, why, whether it is temporary or permanent and what should be done**. 'Overtime 40% over budget because of extra trade and two vacancies' is useful; 'costs were higher this month' is not.
Compare with the **budget, last year and similar firms**. Results that look strong against last year may only reflect an unusually weak year. Comparing with the budget shows whether the plan was met.

head: Chart
Best for
rows: Line chart
A trend over time
Column or bar chart
Comparing items or actual with budget
Pie chart
Each part's share of a total at one time (few parts)
Scatter chart
Whether two measures move together (advertising spend and sales for 20 branches)
Gantt chart
A project timetable (not data analysis)

blocks.note: A red-amber-green dashboard should also show the actual figure and the target, so readers see how far off target each measure is. It must also work when printed in black and white.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every forecast rests on assumptions (sales, price, exchange rate, wage rises). **State them**, with their sources. Never hide an assumption to make a forecast look certain.

**Sensitivity analysis** shows how the result changes if key figures differ from the estimate. Change one figure at a time, for example sales 10% and 20% below plan, or a 5% move in the exchange rate, and show the effect on profit in a small table or chart.

head: Change
Effect on annual profit (J$)
rows: Base case: sales J$40,000,000, contribution 30% (J$12,000,000), fixed costs J$6,000,000
Sales 10% lower (J$36,000,000): contribution J$10,800,000
Sales 20% lower (J$32,000,000): contribution J$9,600,000

blocks.p: Where a small change makes the decision flip (for example profit becomes a loss at 8% lower sales), report this clearly: managers need to know how much room for error there is.

Include factors that numbers do not capture: quality, reliability of suppliers, the effect on customers and staff, the firm's reputation, legal and safety matters, and fit with strategy. Closing a rural branch may save money but harm customers and the firm's name.

ul: Say how reliable each figure is (actual, quote, estimate).
Say what you did not have time to check.
Do not present estimates as facts.

sections.title: Writing and presenting the report; ethics

head: Section
Content
rows: Executive summary (first page)
Purpose, the main findings, the recommendation, and the decision needed
Background and purpose
The decision, the options, the criteria
Analysis
Relevant figures for each option; tables and charts; assumptions
Sensitivity and risks
What changes the answer; non-financial factors
Recommendation
The preferred option, the reasons for it and the next steps
Appendices
Detailed workings and data

ul: Put the **main findings and recommendation at the start**, in an executive summary. If a managing director says the report is too long, **lead with a one-page summary and move detail to appendices**; do not shrink the type or send it twice.
The recommendation section should state the preferred option, the reasons and the next steps, not a full set of working papers or the history of the business.
Use plain language; define technical terms; make tables and charts easy to read and clearly labelled.

Reports on job cuts, a possible purchase of a rival firm or similar matters are **confidential**. Share them only with named readers, mark them confidential, and protect them (passwords, locked storage, numbered copies).

If a staff member asks who will be affected by planned job cuts, keep it confidential and refer him to the proper manager. Do not hint, show the draft in private or tell him because he will find out anyway.
Do not leave copies in meeting rooms, send them to all managers, or give a summary to suppliers or customers.
Follow the organisation's policy and the data protection law.

blocks.p: A report writer must be **honest and objective**. If a manager asks you to show only the figures that favour his preferred option, **present all options and the relevant figures fairly**. Do not bury the others in an appendix few will read, and do not remove figures to avoid an argument. Explain your concern to the manager and, if pressure continues, raise it with your own line manager or follow the organisation's procedure. Do not hide losses, delay bad news or present estimates as facts.

Some months after the decision, compare the actual results with the report's forecast. The purpose is to learn how accurate the forecast was and to improve future reports, not to find someone to blame.

blocks.note: Your professional body's code of ethics (for example, that of the accountancy body in Jamaica) sets out these duties: integrity, objectivity, competence, confidentiality and professional behaviour.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: agree with a manager the decision, readers, deadline and criteria before I start a report.
choose between routine, exception, ad hoc, dashboard and analytical reports.
trace report figures to the records and make sure periods and coding are consistent.
separate relevant costs from sunk, committed and apportioned costs, and include opportunity costs.
calculate contribution and the contribution-to-sales ratio.
report a make-or-buy, special-order, closure, pricing, investment and working-capital decision.
rank products by contribution per unit of a limiting factor and build a plan.
interpret margins, unit costs and variances and explain their causes.
choose a suitable chart or dashboard.
state assumptions, run a sensitivity analysis and add non-financial factors.
write a report with an executive summary and a clear recommendation.
handle confidential reports and resist pressure to mislead.

terms: Management report
A report that helps managers plan, control and decide.
Exception report
A report showing only items outside agreed limits.
Ad hoc report
A one-off report prepared for a particular question.
Relevant cost
A future cash cost that changes as a result of a decision.
Sunk cost
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered and does not change with the decision.
Committed cost
A future cost that must be paid anyway under an earlier agreement.
Avoidable cost
A cost that would be saved if an activity were stopped.
Opportunity cost
The benefit given up by choosing one option instead of another.
Contribution
Selling price less variable cost; the amount each unit adds to fixed costs and profit.
Limiting factor
A scarce resource, such as machine hours, that limits how much a business can produce.
Sensitivity analysis
Testing how a result changes if key figures differ from the estimate.
Executive summary
The short section at the start of a report that gives its main findings and recommendations.
Dashboard
A one-page display of key measures against targets.
Adverse variance
A result worse than budget, such as costs above budget.
Segment
A part of a business, such as a branch, product line or department.

c1.title: Making bottles or buying them: a Clarendon food processor
c1.text: A Clarendon juice processor makes 60,000 bottles a year in its own plant. The variable cost is J$38 a bottle. A further J$12 a bottle of fixed overhead is charged to the plant, but it will continue whether or not the bottles are made. A supplier offers to deliver the same bottles at J$45 each. The plant's equipment could alternatively be rented out for J$150,000 a year.

c2.title: A one-off laundry order
c2.text: A Montego Bay laundry has spare capacity. A hotel offers a one-off contract to wash 8,000 kg of linen at J$200 per kg. The variable cost is J$130 per kg. Fixed costs will not change. The laundry's regular customers pay J$260 per kg. The manager, Mrs Heather Lee, may have to pay overtime of J$40 per kg for part of the work.

c3.title: Scarce machine time at a St Catherine factory
c3.text: A St Catherine plant has 105 machine hours a week. Product Z earns a contribution of J$500 per unit and uses 1 hour; product X earns J$720 and uses 2 hours; product Y earns J$1,050 and uses 3 hours. Weekly demand is 40 units of Z, 25 units of X and any number of Y.

c4.title: The May Pen depot
c4.text: A distributor's May Pen depot has contribution of J$5,400,000 a year and its own fixed costs of J$4,100,000, which would stop if it closed. Head office costs of J$1,800,000 are charged to it, and they will continue whether or not the depot closes. The managing director has asked the accountant for a recommendation.

c5.title: A decision report on new trucks
c5.text: Nadine Brown, an accountant at a Kingston logistics firm, is writing a report for the board on buying three new trucks for J$27,000,000. The firm's fuel and maintenance for the existing fleet cost J$5,460,000 last year over 84,000 km. The transport manager, who wants the purchase, has asked her to leave out a forecast that shows the trucks will not earn enough in the first year.

questions.q: What is the relevant cost of making each bottle?
o: J$50, the variable cost plus the fixed overhead charged
J$38, the variable cost only
J$45, the price the supplier asks
J$12, the fixed overhead per bottle
questions.why: The J$12 fixed overhead continues whatever is decided, so it is not relevant. Only the J$38 that changes with the decision counts.

questions.q: Ignoring the rental option, what is the effect on annual profit of buying the bottles instead of making them?
o: Profit falls by J$420,000
Profit rises by J$420,000
Profit falls by J$720,000
Profit is unchanged
questions.why: Making costs 60,000 x J$38 = J$2,280,000. Buying costs 60,000 x J$45 = J$2,700,000. Buying costs J$420,000 more. Charging J$12 of fixed overhead would give a wrong answer of J$720,000.

questions.q: Now include the opportunity of renting out the equipment for J$150,000 a year if the bottles are bought. What does the report show?
o: Buying is now cheaper, by J$150,000 a year
Buying is now cheaper, by J$270,000 a year
Making is still cheaper, by J$270,000 a year
Making and buying now cost the same
questions.why: If the firm makes the bottles it gives up the rent, so making costs J$2,280,000 + J$150,000 = J$2,430,000. Buying costs J$2,700,000. Making is cheaper by J$270,000.

questions.q: Which non-financial factor should the report also raise?
o: The colour of the supplier's delivery vehicles and uniforms
The age of the furniture in the plant's office block
The number of directors on the supplier's board
The supplier's reliability and quality control
questions.why: Reliability of supply, quality control and delivery times can outweigh a small cost difference. The other factors have no bearing on the decision.

questions.q: Because the laundry has spare capacity and fixed costs will not change, what is the extra profit from the order before any overtime?
questions.why: Contribution per kg = J$200 - J$130 = J$70. 8,000 x J$70 = J$560,000. Check: revenue 1,600,000 - variable cost 1,040,000 = 560,000.

questions.q: What is the contribution-to-sales ratio of the order?
questions.why: Contribution J$70 / price J$200 = 0.35 = 35%.

questions.q: If overtime of J$40 per kg is needed for all 8,000 kg, what is the effect on profit of accepting the order?
o: A gain of J$240,000
A gain of J$560,000
A gain of J$320,000
A loss of J$80,000
questions.why: Overtime adds to variable cost: contribution per kg = 200 - 130 - 40 = J$30. 8,000 x J$30 = J$240,000. The order is still positive but much smaller.

questions.q: Which risk should the report to Mrs Lee mention about accepting the order at J$200?
o: Fixed costs will rise by the same percentage as the new sales
The order will use no electricity or detergent
Regular customers paying J$260 may ask for the same lower price
The hotel will refuse to pay for the work afterwards
questions.why: A price below the normal rate can set a precedent. Fixed costs do not change and the order does use variable inputs, so these are not the risk.

questions.q: In what order should the three products be ranked for use of the machine hours?
o: Z, then X, then Y
Y, then X, then Z, in order of contribution per unit
Z, then Y, then X, because Y earns most per unit
X, then Z, then Y, because X uses a middle number of hours
questions.why: Rank by contribution per machine hour: Z = 500 / 1 = J$500; X = 720 / 2 = J$360; Y = 1,050 / 3 = J$350. X and Y are close, but X is ahead.

questions.q: After meeting the demand for Z and X, how many units of Y can be made?
o: 15 units
35 units
25 units
5 units
questions.why: Z uses 40 x 1 = 40 hours; X uses 25 x 2 = 50 hours; total 90. 105 - 90 = 15 hours left. 15 / 3 hours per unit = 5 units of Y.

questions.q: What is the total weekly contribution from this plan?
A manager says, 'Make as much Y as possible because it has the highest contribution per unit.' What is wrong with this?
o: Y has the lowest contribution per unit of the three products
Contribution per unit is never used in any production plan
Machine time is the limit, and Y earns least per hour
Machine hours should be ignored when choosing between products
questions.why: With a limiting factor, contribution per unit of the scarce resource decides. Making Y first would use hours that earn more on Z and X.

questions.q: What result does the depot's own report show?
o: A profit of J$1,300,000
A loss of J$500,000
A loss of J$1,800,000
A profit of J$5,400,000
questions.why: 5,400,000 - 4,100,000 - 1,800,000 = -500,000. The report charges the head office costs, which is why it shows a loss.

questions.q: What happens to the company's profit if the depot closes?
o: It falls by J$1,300,000
It rises by J$500,000
It rises by J$1,800,000
It is unchanged
questions.why: The company loses the J$5,400,000 contribution and saves only the J$4,100,000 of avoidable fixed costs: a net loss of J$1,300,000. The J$1,800,000 head office costs continue.

questions.q: Why can the depot's profit and loss report mislead the managing director?
o: It uses contribution, which includes some costs that never change
It leaves out the depot's own fixed costs of J$4,100,000
It counts the depot's sales twice in the year's figures
It charges head office costs that will continue anyway
questions.why: Shared costs that will continue are not relevant to the closure decision. Judge it on what is lost (contribution) and what is saved (avoidable costs).

questions.q: Besides the figures, which point should the recommendation raise?
o: The brand of the vehicles that the depot uses for deliveries
The depot's telephone number and the manager's name
Effects on customers, staff and reputation, and other options
The colour and size of the signs outside the depot
questions.why: Decision reports cover non-financial effects, such as loss of customers and jobs, and alternatives such as raising prices or cutting costs.

questions.q: Where should Nadine place her main findings and recommendation?
o: In an appendix at the end of the whole report
Spread through the tables in the analysis section
In a separate email sent after the board meeting has been held
In an executive summary on page one
questions.why: Busy readers start with the summary. Findings and recommendation come first, with workings in appendices.

questions.q: What should Nadine do about the transport manager's request to leave out the unfavourable forecast?
o: Include it, show all options fairly and tell the manager why
Leave it out, since the transport manager understands the trucks best
Put it in a small appendix at the back that few people will read
Leave it out and mention it later in the next quarter's report
questions.why: A report must be honest and complete. Omitting or burying a relevant figure misleads the board. If pressure continues she follows the organisation's procedure.

questions.q: What is the fuel and maintenance cost per kilometre for last year?
The report is based on forecast fuel prices. What should Nadine add so the board can judge the risk?
o: A statement that the fuel forecast is certain and reliable
A list of every one of the fuel invoices paid last year
A table showing the result if fuel prices rise 10% or 20%
A chart of the price of new trucks over the past ten years
questions.why: Sensitivity analysis shows how the result changes when key assumptions differ, so the board sees how much room for error there is.
